“And you, O Jews, have killed. With what did you kill? With the sword of the tongue.”
“It is certainly difficult to remain patient; but one must remember that it takes only one beggar Jew to mock a God on the cross.”
Goethe, letter to Carl Ludwig von Knebel, 12 January 1814. In: Goethe, Werke, Weimar edition, section IV, vol. 24, p. 99.

“Desecration and slaughter by Carl Linfert on NWDR” — On 22 November 1954, Nordwestdeutscher Rundfunk repeated Schmitt’s “Gespräch über die Macht,” which Hessischer Rundfunk had already broadcast on 22 June, now under the title “Macht — so gefährlich wie immer, so verdächtig wie nie” — “Power — As Dangerous as Ever, As Suspect as Never Before.”
Carl Linfert (1900–1981), head of NWDR’s late-night educational programming, introduced the broadcast with a very cautious disclaimer. Schmitt commented on this to Mohler:
“The NWDR broadcast of my conversation was introduced by Carl Linfert, with endless apologies, as though something were about to follow that God had forbidden.”
BW Mohler, p. 183. Schmitt made a similar remark in a letter to Rolf Hinder; see Schmittiana V, 1996, p. 173.

See also G. Giesler’s afterword, p. 80, in C. Schmitt, Gespräch über die Macht und den Zugang zum Machthaber, Stuttgart 2008, and Monika Boll, Nachtprogramm. Intellektuelle Gründungsdebatten in der frühen Bundesrepublik, Münster 2004, p. 103, note 39.
Memor approbii — “I keep the applause in my memory.”

homicidae <fuistis>, et manent — Vulgate, Acts 7:52: “You were murderers.” The early Christian preacher and first martyr Stephen accuses the Jews of murdering the prophets. The addition et manent — “and they remain so” — is not in the Bible and was added by Schmitt.
The biblical passages that follow contain the parable of the workers in the vineyard who kill the vineyard owner’s son in order to seize the inheritance.
Quid timidi estis! Et facta est tranquillitas magna — Vulgate, Matthew 8:26:
et dicit eis quid timidi estis modicae fidei tunc surgens imperavit ventis et mari et facta est tranquillitas magna.
“And he said to them: Why are you afraid, you of little faith? Then he rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.”

“Tarnbruder John” — Otto John (1909–1997), first president of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, from 1950 to 1954. On 20 July 1954 he went to East Germany, probably under duress, and criticized the Federal Republic for the growing influence of former National Socialists.
In 1955 he escaped back to West Berlin, was charged with treason, and sentenced to four years in prison. He was later pardoned. According to current historical understanding, he was innocent.
Ne simus faciles in nominibus — See above, note to p. 15.
Νόμος Basileus — For an explanation of the concept, see Nomos, pp. 42 ff.
“The stump-and-style spirit of Mr. Böhm” — Franz Böhm wrote in the letter mentioned:
“An end to denazification? Good. I would never have started it in the first place.

“But anyone who understands ‘an end to denazification’ to mean the rehabilitation and restoration of the Nazis, their ways of thinking, and their political methods will have to accept that there is a gulf between him and the other Germans greater than the gulf separating us from even the most foreign inhabitants of any country on this planet — indeed, even from enemies of Germany who think justly.

“German is not a biological concept but a spiritual one. It includes sinners and dubious characters of every kind, including criminals. But it does not include people who concern themselves with integrating National Socialism, in any form, into our historical and political tradition …”

“Kojève, Introduction” — Schmitt is referring to Alexandre Kojève, Introduction à la lecture de Hegel. Leçons sur la phénoménologie de l’esprit professées de 1933 à 1939 à l’École des hautes-études, collected and published by Raymond Queneau, Paris 1947; annotated copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 24734.
“he took his own life” — Schmitt gives no page reference, but he is probably referring to the following passage:
The individual “experiences the double meaning contained in what it did, namely that it took its life; it took its own life, but in doing so it rather seized death.”
G. W. F. Hegel, Phänomenologie des Geistes, Sämtliche Werke, ed. H. Glockner, vol. 2, p. 282.

“So eating and drinking can be called a form of knowing” — H.-R. Müller-Schwefe, “Erkenntnis und Wort Gottes.” In: Freundschaftliche Begegnungen. Festschrift für Ernst Jünger zum 60. Geburtstag, ed. Armin Mohler, Frankfurt am Main 1955, pp. 56–74; copy in the Schmitt papers, RW 265 no. 23095.

“Taking, dividing, pasturing” — See C. Schmitt, “Nehmen / Teilen / Weiden. Ein Versuch die Grundfragen jeder Sozial- und Wirtschaftsordnung vom Nomos her richtig zu stellen.” In: VA, pp. 489–504; first published in 1953.

“Gelimer’s laughter” — Gelimer, the last king of the Vandals, was decisively defeated in 533 by the Byzantine general Belisarius, bringing the Vandals’ historical existence to an end. Gelimer responded to the destruction of his kingdom with grim laughter.

Schmitt identified with this reaction as the laughter of a defeated man to such an extent that he gave Book V of the Glossarium the heading “Gelimer.” See the appendix; see also above, p. 371. See BW EJ, pp. 353, 454–55; Reinhard Mehring, “Das Lachen der Besiegten. Das Lachen Gelimers.” In: Zeitschrift für Ideengeschichte 4, 2012, no. 1, pp. 32–45; Martin Tielke, “Habent sua fata libelli et balli.” In: Sinn und Form 64, 2012, pp. 466–67.
“… at 7:45 by taxi to Popitz for the press reception. Saw Hitler and Goebbels. Saw both clearly. Great excitement. Hitler like the greedy bull in the arena. Shaken by that look.”
Tb 1930–34, p. 279. See also Gespräch, p. 105.

H. Recknagel — The commercial lawyer Heinz Recknagel asked Schmitt for the work because the German consul in Malmö, Dr. Meyer, had advised him to read it so that he could better understand the policies of the Soviet Union, where Recknagel had contacts. See his letter to Schmitt of 8 December 1958; RW 265 no. 11334.
Cor ne edito — “Do not eat your heart out”; a proverb meaning: “Don’t worry.” anthropophagus cordis mei — “The devourer of my own heart.”
to E. Forsthoff — Not in BW Forsthoff!

to Kojève, 9 May 1955 — In: Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 101. Kojève, his letter of 2 May 1955 — In: Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 100. Jews who recognized the grotesque insolence of this E. K. — See Kurt Hiller, “Der Fall Erich Kaufmann.” In: idem, Köpfe und Tröpfe, Hamburg 1948, pp. 74–80.

During Kempner’s interrogation of Schmitt, Schmitt’s mention of E. Kaufmann was a tactical chess move. In the Wilhelmstrasse Trial, Kempner later called Kaufmann as a witness and tried to discredit him as a nationalist and militarist; see Carl Schmitt – Antworten in Nürnberg. Edited and annotated by Helmut Quaritsch, Berlin 2000, pp. 42 ff.

Farewell song of the old Moselle man — Under the title “Gesang des alten Mosellaners 1957” (“Song of the Old Moselle Man, 1957”), Schmitt also sent this poem to A. Kojève (see Schmittiana VI, 1998, p. 123) and to A. Mohler (BW Mohler, p. 232). See also the note above on p. 305.
Törwang — A village in Upper Bavaria where E. Forsthoff had a holiday home and where Schmitt visited him in May 1955.

In Göttingen, manly professors have … — When the right-wing nationalist Leonard Schlüter, representing the FDP in the Lower Saxony state government, was appointed Minister of Education and Cultural Affairs at the end of May 1955, the University of Göttingen mounted a major protest. As a result, Schlüter submitted his resignation on 9 June. See Heinz-Georg Marten, Der niedersächsische Ministersturz. Proteste und Widerstand der Georg-August-Universität Göttingen gegen den Kultusminister Schlüter im Jahre 1955, Göttingen 1987. See also Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 108 f.; BW Forsthoff, pp. 502 f.; BW Mohler, p. 200.

“As it thus grasps itself, it is as though the world were only now coming into being for it. Before this, it does not understand the world; it desires it and works upon it, withdraws from it into itself, and destroys it for itself, while also destroying itself as consciousness—as consciousness of the world as essence, and as consciousness of its nothingness. Only here, after the grave of its truth has been lost, and after the destruction of its reality has itself been destroyed … does it discover the world as its new real world.”
G. F. W. Hegel, Werke. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 179.
yesterday I wrote to Kojève — Correctly: on 7 June; see Schmittiana VI, 1998, pp. 108 ff.

to Wirsing — Giselher Wirsing (1907–1975), journalist. In the 1920s he belonged to the Tat circle around Hans Zehrer and, until 1945, served as an editor of various periodicals. In 1948 he was a co-founder of the weekly newspaper Christ und Welt, which he edited as editor-in-chief from 1954 to 1970. During the 1950s, Wirsing was an important supporter of Schmitt in the press. See Kai Burkhardt (ed.), Carl Schmitt und die Öffentlichkeit. Briefwechsel mit Journalisten, Publizisten und Verlegern aus den Jahren 1923 bis 1983, Berlin 2013.
when the jurist Sir Edward Coke told the king … —

“…when Coke said before the king, that ‘his Majesty was defended by the laws,’ James, in anger, told him he spoke foolishly, and he said he was not defended by the laws, but by God (alluding to his ‘divine right’).”

Isaac Disraeli, The Literary Character or, The History of Men of Genius. Drawn from Their Own Feelings and Confessions. Literary Miscellanies; and an Inquiry into the Character of James the First. A new ed. (The Works of Isaac Disraeli, [4]), London etc. 1859, p. 423.

Adolf Caspary — (1898–1953), jurist, emigrated to the United States in 1942. Schmitt had contact with him in 1932 (see Tb 1930–34, p. 184) and refers approvingly above, p. 63, to Caspary’s 1927 book Die Maschinenutopie.

Leo Strauss — (1899–1973), political philosopher. On his relationship with Schmitt, see Heinrich Meier, Carl Schmitt, Leo Strauss und „Der Begriff des Politischen“. Zu einem Dialog unter Abwesenden, 3rd ed., Stuttgart/Weimar 2013.

Walter Benjamin — (1892–1940), philosopher, literary critic, and translator. See Susanne Heil, „Gefährliche Beziehung“. Walter Benjamin und Carl Schmitt, Stuttgart/Weimar 1996; Michael Rumpf (ed.), “Briefwechsel Michael Rumpf – Carl Schmitt.” In: Schmittiana NF II, 2014, pp. 275–285.

under the impact of the words “sacrifice for life …” — Schmitt repeatedly worked through Benjamin’s book on German tragic drama with great intensity; see Reinhard Mehring, “Geist ist das Vermögen, Diktatur auszuüben. Carl Schmitts Marginalien zu Walter Benjamin.” In: idem, Kriegstechniker des Begriffs. Biographische Studien zu Carl Schmitt, Tübingen 2014, pp. 132–152; Jürgen Thaler, “Genial. Carl Schmitt liest Walter Benjamin.” In: Marcel Atze/Volker Kaukoreit (eds.), Lesespuren – Spurenlesen oder Wie kommt die Handschrift ins Buch? Von sprechenden und stummen Annotationen, Vienna 2011, pp. 246–251.
Pleasure conceives and gives birth to sin — 1 John 2:16; see above, p. 315.
Michel Mourre, Lamennais p. 141 — Michel Mourre, Lamennais ou l’hérésie des temps modernes, Paris 1955.
Have I not done exactly the same myself with Adam Müller — In: PR.

The world in which Prof. Wilhelm Grewe’s little light shines — Grewe, who from 1950 onward advised Adenauer in negotiations with the victorious powers of the Second World War, took part in the 1955 trip to Moscow. There he was less willing than Adenauer to make concessions to the Soviets. He is regarded as the originator of the Hallstein Doctrine.

The full-blooded Moju can do that better — This refers to Moritz Julius Bonn, who took part in the negotiations over the Treaty of Versailles as a member of the German delegation in 1919 and was appointed adviser to the Reich Chancellor on reparations in 1920.

Johann Jacob Reiske — (1716–1774), German scholar of Greek, Arabic, and Byzantine studies. In his works, Wilamowitz-Moellendorff repeatedly drew attention to Reiske’s philological achievements, which went unrecognized for many years.
Come along, Cohn — From Theodor Fontane’s poem “An meinem Fünfundsiebzigsten” (“On My Seventy-Fifth Birthday”), which ends:
I was something to everyone, They all read me, They had all known me for ages, And that is the main thing … “come along, Cohn.”

the anti-Roman feeling of the historian Fritz Kern — Kern (1884–1950) became Schmitt’s colleague at the University of Bonn in 1922. On 5 May 1923 Schmitt wrote about him in his diary: “I dislike him; a Protestant professor.” (Tb 1921–24, p. 192). Kern converted to Catholicism in 1949.
“That is the true taking of land” —

“Again and again, from the tangled outlines of the Littorale, the Saracen tower emerged, gradually growing smaller as the perspective changed, a pale shape amid the solitude of rock and sea. At every bend I was glad to see it again, the guardian of a southern territory that had become for me a piece of spiritual homeland. That is the true taking of land.”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 6, p. 315.

Konrad Beyerle — (1872–1933), jurist and politician, co-author of the Weimar Constitution. Article 153 of the Weimar Constitution—corresponding to Article 14 of the German Basic Law—guaranteed property, but also stated:
“Property entails obligations. Its use should also serve the common good.”

This led to a debate lasting several years over the expropriation of the former princely houses. A popular initiative supported expropriation in 1926, but the referendum that followed did not. The attempted expropriation of the princes therefore failed.

My cousin André — André Steinlein (1891–1964), son of the younger brother of Schmitt’s mother, whom Schmitt had known since their school days. On 16 December 1954, Schmitt wrote to Nicolaus Sombart about his ambivalent relationship with him:

“…But I still have to coordinate matters with my Lorraine cousin, an aging bon vivant who, after a typically bourgeois life as a notary, has retreated into a rural backwater on the Seille. Yet, from old habit—we have somehow kept running into one another ever since our youth—I am very fond of him; if only because the old saying applies to him in a typical way: il n’y a pas de notaire qui n’ait rêvé de sultan—there is no notary who has not dreamed of being a sultan.”

Hear the Nobel Prize prophet — This refers to Max Born (1882–1970), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1954. Schmitt is quoting M. Born, “Das entscheidende Motiv. Eine Erwiderung.” In: Merkur, 1955, no. 92, p. 999.
